Menominee Indian Tribe of Wisconsin

The Menominee Indian Tribe of Wisconsin is the named government route, connected to the broader Menominee reading collection. Its public history places the seat of government at Keshena.

Amiskquew, historical Menominee portrait print, c.1843
Amiskquew, c.1843. Lithographic & Print Colouring Establishment; published by Daniel Rice & James G. Clark, Philadelphia. Library of Congress,95502208,pga.07485. McKenney & Hall are catalogued contributors; individual portrait artist not identified in the inspected LOC record. No known restrictions on publication.

These are selected starting points. The full annotated collection, source perspectives, inspection limits and remaining research questions follow below. A starting guide is not an exhaustive history or community endorsement.

01

A government within continuing communities

The Tribe’s account locates its government at Keshena and names Neopit, Middle Village, Zoar and South Branch alongside it. It describes housing and infrastructure pressures as community concerns. The undated page’s figures are not current measurements.

Read the sources [1] Menominee Indian Tribe of Wisconsin

02

A public museum account in the Tribe’s voice

The Cultural Museum introduces the homeland through the Tribe’s account of endurance, leadership and continuing language and tradition. This is a public institutional narrative. Its linked tours and object videos have not been reviewed, and public presentation does not establish a blanket right to reproduce collection images or restricted knowledge.

Read the sources [2] Menominee Indian Tribe of Wisconsin
